10 units, each with worked examples, a 10-mark practice set in CBSE question styles, common mistakes and quick recall

How this book matches your board exam. Research check: this book follows NCERT Class 12 Chemistry Part 1, Unit 1 (Solutions), for the CBSE 2026–27 session. The Chemistry theory paper is 70 marks in 3 hours, with 30 marks for practicals. Solutions carries about 7 marks. Recent sample papers have 33 questions in five sections: A — 16 one-mark items (MCQs and assertion–reason); B — 5 two-mark; C — 7 three-mark; D — 2 four-mark case-based; E — 3 five-mark. The syllabus covers types of solutions, concentration terms, solubility of gases (Henry's law), Raoult's law, ideal and non-ideal solutions, colligative properties (relative lowering of vapour pressure, elevation of boiling point, depression of freezing point, osmotic pressure), determination of molar mass, and abnormal molar mass with the van 't Hoff factor.

Each unit ends with a 10-mark practice set. Constants: R = 0.0821 L atm mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ (= 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹); for water, K_b = 0.52 K kg mol⁻¹, K_f = 1.86 K kg mol⁻¹. Every numerical answer was checked by computer. The marking points are our own, not the official CBSE marking scheme.

Unit 1 of 10: Types of Solutions and Concentration Terms

Key ideas

  • A solution is a homogeneous mixture of two or more components; the component in larger amount is the solvent. Binary solutions can be solid, liquid or gaseous (e.g. amalgam of mercury with sodium — liquid in solid; oxygen in water — gas in liquid).
  • Concentration terms:
  • mass percentage = (mass of component / total mass) × 100;
  • ppm = (parts of component / total parts) × 10⁶;
  • mole fraction x_A = n_A / (n_A + n_B); Σx = 1;
  • molarity M = moles of solute / volume of solution in L (depends on temperature);
  • molality m = moles of solute / mass of solvent in kg (independent of temperature).

Worked examples

Example 1: 4 g NaOH (M = 40) in 250 mL solution: M = 0.1/0.25 = 0.4 M.

Example 2: 9 g glucose (M = 180) in 250 g water: m = 0.05/0.25 = 0.2 mol kg⁻¹.

Example 3: 46 g ethanol (1 mol) + 54 g water (3 mol): x_ethanol = 0.25.

10-mark practice set

  1. (1 mark, MCQ) Which concentration term is independent of temperature? (a) molarity (b) molality (c) normality (d) % w/v. Answer: (b).
  2. (1 mark) Why does molarity change with temperature? Answer: the volume of the solution changes with temperature.
  3. (2 marks) Find the molality of a solution of 5.85 g NaCl (M = 58.5) in 500 g water. Answer: n = 0.1 mol (1); m = 0.2 mol kg⁻¹ (1).
  4. (3 marks) A solution contains 20 g of urea (M = 60) in 180 g of water. Find the mole fraction of urea and the mass percentage. Answer: n_urea = 0.333, n_water = 10 (1); x_urea = 0.333/10.333 ≈ 0.032 (1); mass % = 20/200 × 100 = 10% (1).
  5. (3 marks) Concentrated HNO₃ is 68% by mass with density 1.504 g/mL. Find its molarity (M = 63). Answer: 1 L = 1504 g, HNO₃ = 0.68 × 1504 = 1022.7 g (1); moles = 16.23 (1); molarity ≈ 16.2 M (1).

Common mistakes

  1. Using solution mass for molality. 2. mL not converted to L. 3. Mole fractions not adding to 1. 4. Wrong molar masses. 5. Confusing molarity and molality.

Quick recall

  1. Molarity? 2. Molality? 3. Σ mole fractions? 4. ppm? 5. Temperature-independent terms?

Answers: 1) mol/L solution. 2) mol/kg solvent. 3) 1. 4) parts per million. 5) Molality, mole fraction, mass %.
